Jill Davis's official work week starts Monday morning. Unofficially, it kicks off every Sunday afternoon when, like clockwork, anxious thoughts begin seeping into her brain.

"Am I organized and ready enough? Am I prepared for this meeting?" says Davis, the chief development officer at a nonprofit. To bat the angst away, she'll often launch into work, writing emails and saving them as drafts so she doesn't disturb her colleagues.

Chances are they're already fretting about work, too. The "Sunday scares" have become such a fixture of Americans' weekends that Merriam-Webster added the term to its online dictionary last month. Its definition: a feeling of anxiety or sadness one may feel when the weekend is almost over, either because the work/school week is about to begin, there is no more time for fun or relaxing weekend activities, or both.

That pre-Monday dread isn't a new phenomenon, but there's reason to believe it is intensifying as workloads mount and job security ebbs. More than half of U.S. workers say they experience
